name: collection-pipeline
intent: Organise a computation over a collection as a chain of operations that each take a collection and emit the next one (map, filter, flatMap, group), ending in a terminal operation that produces a single value, so the flow of data is stated declaratively instead of being encoded in loop bookkeeping.
problem: A loop that processes a collection mixes three decisions at once: how to iterate, what to select or transform, and what to accumulate - so every variant of the task becomes a new loop with its own index, temporary list and mutation. Adding, removing or reordering a processing step means editing the loop body, the intermediate state has to be declared and filled by hand, and the intent ('the active users' e-mails, deduplicated, sorted, first ten') is spread across the loop instead of being readable in one expression.
context: Per-element processing of in-memory or streamed collections where the transformations compose linearly: data cleaning and shaping, report aggregation, rule evaluation over lists, grouping and joining, and any place where the same sequence of operations is applied to different inputs. It pays off when the language has first-class functions plus a collection library with map/filter/reduce (or comprehensions, streams, iterators, sequences), because the clarity comes from lambdas; it applies to lazy sources (iterators, file handles, unbounded sequences) as well as to materialised collections, provided the stages are pure enough to be re-evaluated.
benefits: Intent is visible in the code: 'take the active people, map to their e-mail, deduplicate, sort, take ten' reads in data-flow order instead of having to be reconstructed from index arithmetic and a mutable accumulator.
Stages are small, named, independently testable functions; the chain can be reordered, extracted into a named pipeline, or applied to a different input without touching a loop.
Loop bookkeeping disappears - no index variables, no manual 'add to result' branch, no temporary collections to declare - which removes a whole class of off-by-one and wrong-accumulator bugs.

The same shape works over different sources because the operations are defined on the collection abstraction (List, IEnumerable, Stream, Sequence, Iterator, Iterable), so one pipeline can read an array, a file, a database cursor or a stream.
Composition is modular at the operation level: where a loop fuses several concerns, the pipeline names each concern as one stage, so a change stays local to that stage.

Lazy pipelines (views, sequences, lazy enumerators, iterators, streams) evaluate in a single pass without materialising intermediate collections, can stop early through short-circuiting terminals (take/find/any), and can read sources that do not fit in memory.
tradeoffs: An eager chain allocates one intermediate collection per stage: a five-stage pipeline over a million rows produces five collections that a single fused loop would never create, so the pattern is a size-dependent performance bet unless the runtime is lazy.

Laziness changes semantics, not just timing: the work happens when the terminal operation runs, side effects inside stages are deferred and reordered, a lazy view iterated twice re-runs its stages, and a transformation that is read once per element cannot be cached.

Pipelines are one-shot values in most runtimes - a consumed iterator, stream or lazy enumerator cannot be re-traversed (a Java stream may even throw IllegalStateException on reuse), so the chain is not a reusable collection unless it is materialised deliberately.

Debugging is harder than in a loop: stack traces point into library internals or anonymous lambdas, 'step to the next element' has no uniform meaning, and a failing element is identified only by the position of the stage.

Parallelism is only safe for stateless, associative stages (parallel streams, PLINQ, rayon, parallel collections): an element function that shares mutable state produces silent races, and results may arrive out of order unless ordering is re-imposed.

Longer chains degrade type inference and diagnostics (Java wildcard capture, TypeScript inference on generic callbacks, Rust closure lifetimes pointing at the adapter), and error handling has no natural stage: an exception aborts the pipeline, and a stage that may fail or skip needs explicit lifting.

Multi-input, branching or stateful stages do not fit the linear model; grouping, joining and windowing read worse as a chain, and the pipeline can hide per-element costs (a lookup or sort inside a filter) that a loop would have made obvious.

Stateful operations (sorted, distinct, limit on large streams) require buffering O(N) elements or more, which undermines the memory advantage of laziness and can become a performance cliff rather than an incremental cost.

participants.responsibility: The collection, array, iterator, stream, sequence or generator that supplies the elements; it may be materialised (a list) or lazy (an iterator, a file, an unbounded sequence).

A per-element transformation that takes a collection and emits the next one: map/select (transform each element), filter/where (drop elements), flatMap/flatten (expand one element into many), plus the positional stages distinct, sort, group.

The caller-supplied lambda or function reference that gives a stage its concrete behaviour (the predicate of a filter, the transform of a map, the combining function of a reduce); it should be small and free of side effects.
The last operation, which consumes the pipeline and produces a single value or a side effect: reduce/fold/inject, collect, sum, count, find, any/all, forEach.

The composed chain itself - an ordered, nameable value that can be stored, passed, applied to another source or reused; it also carries the runtime's laziness/eagerness policy (views, sequences, lazy enumerators, streams).
Requests the result, owns all I/O, and decides what to do with it; it is the only place that triggers evaluation of a lazy pipeline.

use_cases: ETL and report shaping: drop invalid rows, normalise fields, group by key and reduce to totals before the result is persisted or returned.
Query-like filtering of in-memory domain objects: select a customer's orders for a period, map them to line items and sum the amounts, instead of writing nested loops with accumulators.
Streaming over large or unbounded input: read a log file line by line, parse, filter and aggregate without materialising the file (lazy sequences, iterators, streams, AsyncSequence).
Refactoring existing loops: Fowler's documented route from a loop to a pipeline - split the loop, extract the per-element logic, then express it as filter/map/collect stages.
Bulk validation and projection of message batches, where each element is handled independently and failures are collected per element rather than aborting the batch.
Configuration and argument assembly: normalise, deduplicate, sort and cap a list of names, tags or flags before use.
Database or API result post-processing: project entities into DTOs, group them, and compute per-group aggregates at the edge instead of shipping raw rows further.

Reactive stream processing: RxJS observables, RxJava streams, or Reactor pipelines handling sequences of UI events, HTTP responses, or message queue payloads as declarative pipelines with backpressure.
Streaming analytics: continuous aggregation of metrics from unbounded log streams, sensor readings, or financial tickers where late-arriving data must be windowed and re-aggregated.

ML preprocessing pipelines: normalise features, encode categoricals, split train/test splits, and apply feature transforms as a composable, testable sequence of pure functions over data frames or record arrays.

Distributed data processing: Apache Spark DataFrame pipelines chain lazy transformations (select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, join) into a logical plan that the Catalyst optimizer compiles into fused pipelined execution only when an action (show, count, collect, write) triggers evaluation.

Functional data processing on the BEAM: Elixir pipes an enumerable through Enum for eager per-step lists or through Stream for a lazy computation graph - 1..100_000 |> Stream.map(&(&1 * 3)) |> Stream.filter(&odd?/1) |> Enum.sum() - with the documented guidance to start with Enum and move to Stream for large or potentially infinite sources.

Whole-frame analytics in Python: pandas DataFrame.pipe composes custom and built-in steps as df.pipe(read).pipe(clean).pipe(derive, unit='kg'), passing the frame as the first argument (or a named keyword via a (callable, 'kw') tuple) so user-defined stages chain like built-in methods.
avoid_when: The loop performs several unrelated jobs at once (two aggregates, or one aggregate plus mutation of shared state): split the loop first, or write the explicit passes - forcing one pipeline hides the second concern.

The language has no first-class functions or collection library to build on (see the C entry): emulating lambda-per-stage with one-method classes or function pointers plus a void* context produces code messier than the loop it replaces.

The transformation is inherently index-dependent or stateful (in-place mutation, sliding windows over shared state, algorithms that need the previous element's position): an explicit loop states that better.

A measured hot path runs the pipeline per element or the chain is three stages over a tiny collection: the per-stage indirection and intermediate collections can dominate, and a fused hand-written loop is legitimate there.
The only 'stage' is a side effect (`forEach` with logging, remote calls or mutation): that is an imperative loop wearing a pipeline costume, and the ordering should be visible.
Error handling must differ per element and the language's library cannot lift failures (no Result/Option-aware stage, no try_collect): a plain loop with explicit error collection is clearer.

The pipeline would require nested or multi-branch control flow (cross-stage coordination, per-stage exception recovery, or dynamic stage selection): a custom orchestrator or state machine is clearer than forcing it into a linear chain.
anti_patterns: Pipeline as a for-loop in disguise: a chain whose only purpose is a forEach with side effects (logging, mutation, remote calls) - the data flow reads as declarative while the ordering that really matters is invisible.
One enormous expression: a twenty-call chain with no extracted methods, kept on one line 'to use the pipeline', instead of naming each sub-task as a function.
Hidden per-element cost: a lookup, a sort or a network call inside a filter/map so the pipeline conceals that the expensive operation runs once per element.
Non-lazy chains over large inputs that materialise list after list, presented as streaming.
Reusing a consumed stream/iterator/lazy sequence, or iterating a lazy view twice and expecting cached results.
Mixing comprehension form and pipeline form in the same expression until nobody can see where the data goes or where it is materialised.

Parallel stream on I/O-bound work: using parallelStream for network calls, database queries, or file reads where threads block on I/O, starving the shared ForkJoinPool and degrading overall throughput. Use virtual threads (Java 21+) or CompletableFuture for I/O concurrency instead.
Chaining stream().filter().findFirst() on a Map for key lookup: this is O(n) vs the O(1) map.get(key) operation, and becomes a hot spot in profilers under load.
design_principles: Declarative over imperative: describe the transformation, not the traversal; the runtime owns how the elements are visited.
Single responsibility and small functions: each stage does one thing at one level of abstraction, and a stage worth naming is worth extracting.
Composition over inheritance: behaviour is built by chaining functions, not by subclassing a processing framework.
Purity at the boundaries: element functions stay side-effect free so the chain remains reorderable and laziness stays safe; effects belong to the consumer.
Open/closed at the stage level: new behaviour arrives as a new or reordered stage, not as an edit inside an existing one.
Let the runtime own traversal policy: short-circuiting, laziness and parallelism are runtime decisions, so the pipeline must not depend on evaluation order.
Idempotency at every stage: filters and transformers should be safe to re-execute, which matters in streaming pipelines where a stage may see the same element after a downstream failure and retry.
best_practices: Build the pipeline in small steps - start from the narrowest source, add one stage, check the shape and type of the intermediate result - which is Fowler's own advice for longer pipelines.
Extract a method as soon as a group of stages has a name, keep chains linear and short (roughly under half a dozen stages), and name the chain once if it is used more than once.

Choose the evaluation policy deliberately: lazy sequences/views/iterators for large, chained or unbounded input; materialise (toList/collect/force) when the result must outlive the pipeline or be traversed again.
Keep element functions small, pure and I/O-free; put logging, metrics and remote calls in the consumer or in a single explicitly named terminal stage.
Decide the terminal operation before writing the stages - a single value (reduce/fold/sum/find) or a collection - and let that choice determine the last stage.
Order stages cheaply: filter before map, limit early, avoid re-sorting, and keep parallel pipelines stateless and associative with ordering re-imposed explicitly when it matters.
Test the stages individually and the assembled pipeline end to end, including the empty, single-element and short-circuiting cases; never test the pipeline's internals.

Use primitive specialised streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream) for numeric aggregation; boxed Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long> carries an order-of-magnitude allocation cost per element on tight numeric loops.

Prefer collect() over forEach+shared mutable state in both sequential and parallel pipelines; forEach with a shared ArrayList or HashMap is a data race under parallelism and produces silent corruption.

Apply the N*Q model before reaching for parallel streams: parallelism overhead pays off only when N (element count) multiplied by Q (per-element cost) exceeds roughly 10,000; profile before parallelising.

Use Collector.teeing() (Java 12+) or equivalent fan-out collectors when the same pass must compute two or more independent aggregates; traversing the source twice for separate reduce operations is a wasteful regression.

Place size-reducing operations (filter, skip, limit, distinct) before expensive per-element operations (map with heavy computation, sorted, flatMap); this is not premature optimisation - it changes algorithmic complexity.

Never place sorted() before a short-circuiting terminal; use min()/max() with a comparator when you need the smallest or largest element, as sorted() must materialise the entire upstream before emitting anything.

Use peek() exclusively for debugging; remove it from production pipelines or replace it with a dedicated side-effect stage with an explicit comment, as peek() can be silently removed by some optimisers and its behaviour is unspecified under parallel unordered execution.

For stateful transformations inside lazy streams (sliding windows, running totals, conditional grouping), prefer built-in stateful pipeline operators (Java Stream.gather() with windowSliding/scan, Kotlin windowedBy, RxJS scan) over manual mutable-accumulators inside map.

Custom ForkJoinPool: isolate long-running parallel streams from the shared common pool in server applications; a custom pool with a fixed thread count (e.g. new ForkJoinPool(Runtime.availableProcessors() / 2)) prevents pipeline work from starving other parallel tasks.

Declare Collector characteristics (UNORDERED, CONCURRENT, IDENTITY_FINISH) correctly; UNORDERED enables parallel optimisation for distinct() and groupingBy(); CONCURRENT requires a thread-safe accumulator and permits a single shared accumulator rather than per-thread copies.

In reactive stream pipelines (RxJS, Reactor, Flow): flatten nested observables with switchMap/mergeMap/exhaustMap rather than subscribing inside a map, and always use debounceTime before switchMap on search inputs to avoid flooding the pipeline.
sources: Martin Fowler, Collection Pipeline (2015): https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/collection-pipeline/ - the pattern's origin, named as a special case of Pipes and Filters and as a case of composing higher-order functions over sequence data. Fowler traces the pattern to Smalltalk's collection library and argues it died out for mainstream OO only because C++, Java and C# lacked clean lambda syntax until Java 8 and C# 3.

Martin Fowler, Refactoring with Loops and Collection Pipelines (2015): https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/refactoring-pipelines.html - the documented refactoring route: Split Loop, Extract Method on the loop body, then filter/map/collect stages. Also covers when list comprehensions are a viable alternative and why SQL-like transformations make pipelines amenable to query push-down.

Martin Fowler, Operation Catalog (map, filter, reduce, flat-map, sort): https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/collection-pipeline/reduce.html - detailed operation descriptions including reduce semantics, left vs right fold, and the choice between named functions vs lambdas for reduction.

Oracle, java.util.stream package summary (Java 21): https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/stream/package-summary.html - the JDK's stream pipeline contract: source, intermediate operations (always lazy), terminal operation, reduction semantics, collector contract, and characteristics (CONCURRENT, UNORDERED, IDENTITY_FINISH).

BackendBytes, Java Streams: Pipeline Internals, Performance Traps, and Production Patterns (2026): https://backendbytes.com/articles/java-streams-api-practical-guide/ - covers pipeline fusion, primitive stream boxing penalties (10x for Stream<Integer> vs IntStream), N*Q parallelism model, sorted() eager-materialisation, teeing(), ForkJoinPool isolation, and the specific conditions under which parallel streams actually improve performance.

Baeldung, When to Use a Parallel Stream in Java (2025): https://www.baeldung.com/java-when-to-use-parallel-stream - covers the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() default, per-element cost and dataset size thresholds, spliterability, stateful behavioural parameters, and why side-effect accumulation inside parallel streams is unsafe.

InfoWorld, High-Performance Programming with Java Streams (2025): https://infoworld.media/article/4091427/high-performance-programming-with-java-streams.html - covers stream gatherers (Java 22+), windowSliding, scan, mapConcurrent for virtual-thread-friendly concurrency, zip(), short-circuiting, and the distinction between parallel streams (CPU-bound data parallelism) vs virtual threads (massive I/O concurrency).

Kindatechnical, Functional Data Pipelines with Python (2026): https://kindatechnical.com/functional-programming/functional-data-pipelines-with-python.html - pure-function generator pipelines, Result types for error propagation, parallel_map with multiprocessing.Pool, batch() for chunked ETL, and why each stage as Iterable[A]->Iterable[B] composition enables trivial unit testing.

Software Patterns Lexicon, Pipeline Pattern in Python (2024): https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/python/functional-design-patterns/pipeline-pattern/ - Python-specific pipeline idioms: functions for pure transforms, callable objects for configured stages, generators for streaming, Protocols for stage contracts, and async pipeline patterns with asyncio.

Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Pipes and Filters Pattern: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/pipes-and-filters - the architectural sibling of Collection Pipeline: independent filter processing units, idempotency requirements, duplicate message detection, and error handling strategies for distributed pipeline deployments.

StackPractices, Pipes and Filters Pattern (2026): https://stackpractices.com/patterns/pipes-and-filters-pattern/ - practical implementation variants: synchronous, async, parallel, streaming, and batch pipelines; filter purity guidelines; builder-based dynamic pipeline construction; and Chain-of-Responsibility distinction.

InfoQ, RxJS Best Practices in Angular 16 (2025): https://www.infoq.com/articles/rxjs-angular16-best-practices/ - flattening operators (switchMap, mergeMap, exhaustMap), AsyncPipe for subscription management, debounceTime on search inputs, signals vs observables for local vs async state, and catchError/retry for resilient stream pipelines.

Java Design Patterns, Collection Pipeline: https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/collection-pipeline/ - Java-specific pattern overview with assembly-line metaphor, Java 8 Stream API examples (filter, sorted, groupBy, flatMap), and a suitability checklist.

Gill et al., 'A Shortcut to Deforestation' (1993) - the foldr/build fusion law that avoids intermediate list allocation by fusing a producer (build) with a consumer (foldr) into a single recursive function; foundational result for stream fusion and deforestation in Haskell GHC.

Coutts et al., 'Stream Fusion' (2007) - improved deforestation technique that handles zips and left folds, implemented in GHC's stream fusion rewrite rules, enabling Haskell to compile list pipelines to equivalent fused loops.

Apache Software Foundation, pyspark.sql.DataFrame API reference: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.DataFrame.html - DataFrame transformations (select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, join) are lazy: each returns a new immutable DataFrame and builds a logical plan executed only when an action (show, collect, count, write) is invoked.

Apache Software Foundation, Spark ML Pipelines (4.1/4.2 docs): https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/ml-pipeline.html - Pipeline as an ordered sequence of Transformer/Estimator stages that flow DataFrames through transform()/fit(); the fitted PipelineModel is itself a Transformer that applies the whole chain to new data.

Elixir Team, Enumerables and Streams: https://hexdocs.pm/elixir/enumerable-and-streams.html - the Enum/Stream duality: Enum functions traverse eagerly and build an intermediate list per pipeline step, while Stream builds a lazy computation graph realised only when consumed; the documented guidance is Enum first, Stream for large or infinite collections.

pandas project, DataFrame.pipe API (pandas 3.0 docs): https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pipe.html - chainable application of functions that expect the DataFrame as first argument (or via a (callable, data_keyword) tuple), documented as the clean way to compose a sequence of whole-frame transformations with groupby/resampler variants.

Java Coder, Functional Java: Please Stop Writing Unreadable Streams (2025): https://javacoder.org/functional-java-please-stop-writing-unreadable-streams/ - misuse critique of pipeline overuse: multi-line block lambdas, side effects inside predicates, nested chains; prescribes extracting named methods per stage (isPending, safeEnrichOrder) and keeping the chain readable as filter -> map -> collect.

MIT 6.005, Reading: Map, Filter, Reduce: https://web.mit.edu/6.005/www/fa16/classes/24-map-filter-reduce/ - course reading presenting the collection-pipeline abstraction: operating on sequences via map/filter/reduce instead of explicit loops and conditionals, with the abstraction rationale (which elements, transformed how, combined how) made explicit.
